analysis.one_liner: Sets tightening methane limits on oil and gas facilities and bans routine flaring by 2030.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote, a floor vote, or a single cosponsor, and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the EPA to set methane emissions limits for oil and gas facilities, with the limits getting tighter every three years toward a goal of cutting total methane emissions 90% by 2030 compared to 2015. It would have phased out routine flaring, the practice of burning off excess natural gas, almost completely by 2030, and required facility operators to run leak detection and repair programs. It also laid groundwork for a system where facilities that emit less than the limit could sell credits to those that emit more, and funded studies to verify emissions measurements.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near oil and gas facilities, whose air quality is affected by methane leaks and flaring, and the public broadly, since methane is a potent greenhouse gas driving climate change. Companies that make emissions-detection technology, such as sensor, drone, and satellite systems, would gain a large new mandated market. Producers that already operate cleanly could also profit by selling compliance credits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities near gas facilities and the public

how_it_helps.text: Directs the EPA to set methane intensity standards for oil and gas facilities that become more stringent every three years, aimed at cutting total methane emissions 90% below 2015 levels by 2030 [S2][S3].
Requires regulations to phase out routine flaring of natural gas, cutting nationwide flaring emissions at least 80% below 2017 levels by 2028 and eliminating them by 2030 [S2][S3].
Requires every covered facility to file a leak detection and repair plan specifying its inspection technology, inspection frequency, and repair schedule [S3].
Creates a national public methane emissions database and requires verification procedures so reported emissions data can be checked for accuracy [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas producers, who would bear the cost of upgrading equipment, monitoring emissions continuously, repairing leaks, and ending routine flaring. Some of those costs could be passed to consumers through energy prices. The bill would also displace the EPA's existing Clean Air Act methane standards for covered facilities with this new framework, which would take up to four years to issue initial standards.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas producers, possibly energy consumers

drawbacks.text: The bill would bar the EPA from enforcing its existing Clean Air Act section 111 methane standards at covered facilities, and initial standards under the new framework would not be due until four years after enactment, so near-term rules would loosen before the new ones arrive [S3].

The tradable credits program, if activated, would let high-emitting facilities keep polluting by buying credits from cleaner operators, and it would only go into effect if the EPA first determined that commercial monitoring technology is accurate enough to support it [S2][S3].
Compliance costs for producers and the flaring phase-out could raise costs in the natural gas supply chain, some portion of which reaches consumers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefits are real and large in scale: methane is one of the most powerful greenhouse gases, and flaring and leaks also put pollutants into the air near drilling sites. The main honest objections are timing and flexibility: the bill would pause existing EPA methane enforcement for up to four years while new standards are written, and its credit-trading mechanism would depend on measurement technology that the EPA itself would have to verify. The costs fall on a specific, highly profitable industry, with an uncertain pass-through to energy prices.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees the day it was introduced and sent to a subcommittee the next day, but neither ever acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Scott Peters introduced the bill on April 22, 2021 [S1][S5].

It was referred the same day to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Foreign Affairs Committee, and on April 23 it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Environment and Climate Change [S5].
The bill attracted zero cosponsors in the House [S4].
No committee markup, report, or floor action ever followed, and the bill expired at the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers came out ahead, because no federal methane intensity standards or routine flaring ban in this form was ever enacted, and they faced no compliance costs from this bill. The public got nothing from it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas producers avoided new methane rules

for.name: Rep. Scott H. Peters
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, which set methane intensity standards, a flaring phase-out, and leak detection requirements for oil and gas facilities.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Environment and Climate Change and never held a markup or advanced it to the floor during the two-year Congress.

against.name: House Foreign Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action on it before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever recorded and not a single member of either party signed on as a cosponsor, so no partisan pattern was ever visible on the bill itself [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would have imposed declining methane intensity standards, a leak detection and repair mandate, and an end to routine flaring by 2030, all of which require capital spending by producers. The industry's interest here ran against the public's interest in cutting a potent greenhouse gas and reducing local air pollution. The bill died without a vote, so no costs were ever imposed.

industries.industry: Emissions detection and monitoring technology companies
industries.note: The bill would have mandated leak detection plans at every covered facility, funded studies of measurement methods, and set testing protocols for sensors, drones, aircraft, and satellite systems, creating a large mandated market for this technology. Its fortunes depended entirely on the bill advancing, and it did not.

industries.industry: Natural gas marketers and LNG exporters
industries.note: The bill would have created a national registry to calculate the methane intensity of gas delivered to end users and LNG exporters, which could have let sellers certify lower-carbon gas to buyers. That same registry would also have made supply-chain emissions visible to the public.
